notes.coinbase_maturity: The size of the maturity ring, indexed by height modulo this value. Zero divides by zero inside the fold on every block (I1-L11).
notes.emission_decay_divisor: One part per epoch. 1054 with a 2880-block epoch compounds to a yearly factor of 0.70702, which is to say the rate halves every two years (I1-L2). The decaying arm runs over epochs 0 through 4375 and sums to a pre-tail supply of 62,744,838.47 ZCD, of which 62,744,817.47 is actually issued because the genesis block pays no coinbase; the tail takes over at epoch 4376, height 12,602,880. Do not quote epoch_length * genesis_emission * this: that product is 63,745,920 ZCD, the sum of the INFINITE geometric decay, and it overshoots the finite schedule by 1.6% -- it is an upper bound and was carried here as the value until #394. Either figure is what the curve sums to, not a cap it guarantees to reach, because a coinbase burned under I1-M2 is a permanent shortfall the schedule never repays.
notes.treasury_share_bps: The fraction of every block subsidy credited to the treasury cell (whitepaper 14.1), the remainder paying consensus. On the subsidy only, never on fees. The floor goes to the treasury and the remainder to the producer, so the two always sum to the subsidy exactly.
notes.pow_engine: The work function this network requires, matched against the engine the running binary was built with; a mismatch is a refusal to start, in both directions. It is in the consensus root because that is what it is -- a network is defined by the function its headers are proved against, and two chains agreeing on every other parameter and disagreeing here are not the same chain. The job no comment could do: RandomX is compiled behind a build tag, so a binary built without it holds only the development engine, and a development engine pointed at this network would accept one BLAKE3 pass as proof of work for every header it ever saw. Devnet declares dev-blake3 for the same reason from the other side.
notes.randomx_key_interval: The proof-of-work key schedule: re-key every randomx_key_interval blocks, with randomx_key_lag blocks of slack in the epoch arithmetic so the key for any height is settled long before that height is mined. Validate requires the lag strictly below the interval -- at or above it the arithmetic stops shifting the interval boundary and starts skipping epochs, so the schedule would no longer re-key every interval, which is the one thing the pair is for. THE KEY IS DERIVED FROM THE HEIGHT AND THE CHAIN ID, NOT FROM A KEY BLOCK'S HASH, and that is a deliberate departure from upstream RandomX's own schedule. What it buys: pow.CheckWork stays a TOTAL function of a header's bytes, so a header whose ancestry this node does not hold still has checkable work -- which orphan admission, announcement scoring and a work cache keyed by block id all rest on, and which whitepaper §3's stateless-verification claim rests on too. It also removes a grinding vector upstream's schedule admits, where the miner of a key block can grind its own hash to influence the next epoch's key. WHAT IT COSTS: every key of every epoch is known from genesis, which breaks the key-unpredictability premise upstream assumes. Dataset precomputation is NOT the concern -- it is symmetric, honest miners precompute equally, and it improves liveness at a key boundary. The concern is long-horizon offline specialisation, since part of RandomX's ASIC-resistance argument is that a chip or a superoptimiser cannot prepare for future keys. The per-key gain is small in the literature because programs depend on key AND nonce, but it is exactly the kind of assumption upstream does not guarantee. It is defensible here because proof of work is a distribution mechanism with an expiry date rather than permanent consensus; THE RISK GROWS WITH THE LENGTH OF THE PoW-TO-PoS RAMP, so lengthening the ramp reopens this decision, and the reversal trigger is evidence of specialised hardware rather than a calendar review. The full entry is ARCHITECTURE §21 and the comment on pow.KeyFor.
notes.max_target: The absolute ceiling on the proof-of-work target: the easiest difficulty the chain may ever reach (F-PARAM-1). The difficulty rule clamps relatively, at +/- difficulty_clamp_factor per block, which bounds the step and not the destination; with saturating 256-bit arithmetic, sustained upward pressure walks the target to 2^256-1, where CheckWork accepts every hash and BlockWork returns 1 for every header, so fork choice becomes a block count. 2^250 is 2^12 = 4096x of headroom above genesis_target = 2^238 — more than any plausible hashrate collapse the LWMA needs to absorb — while keeping BlockWork at 63: floor(2^256 / (2^250 + 1)) = 63, not 64, because 64 * (2^250 + 1) > 2^256. A header at the ceiling therefore still costs about 64 expected hashes (2^256 / (2^250 + 1)) rather than one, and block work remains a six-bit measurement rather than a bit. Validate requires genesis_target <= max_target and max_target < 2^255, the point at which block work collapses to one.
notes.future_time_limit_seconds: How far ahead of a node's own clock a block's timestamp may be before the node withholds it rather than judging it (R1-H2, wire.md §9 rule 8). Withholding — not rejecting — is what keeps wall clocks from forking validity, and it is what bounds the median-time push that drove issue #70's freeze. IT BOUNDS THE DOWNWARD COLLAPSE AND ONLY THAT: with the bound in place #70's push reaches a worst real block interval of about 53 s on mainnet and 92 s on devnet, against roughly 48 years unbounded. THE MIRROR DIRECTION IS BOUNDED BY THE CONTROLLER AND NOT BY THIS PARAMETER, and both halves of that fix have landed. The mechanism, for the record, because the number below is still quoted: a miner dating every block it wins at now + this - 1 is never withheld and never scored, and while NextTarget floored solve times at zero the honest block after it contributed zero instead of the compensating negative, so the inflation was (this - 1) per attacker block, cumulatively, with a fixed point only for an attacker share p < target_block_seconds / future_time_limit_seconds — 16.7% at 30 / 180, and 2.8% on devnet's 5 s goal against the same 180 s limit, since THE THRESHOLD SCALED WITH target_block_seconds AND NOT WITH THIS VALUE ALONE. THAT THRESHOLD IS HISTORY AND NOT A PROPERTY OF THE SHIPPED RULE. #30 signed the accumulator and clamped it symmetrically, so the honest block now contributes the negative that cancels the donation and the free ratchet is gone: sim/timestamp_test.go drives the real rule at 10%, 16%, 17%, 25% and 50% on mainnet and at 1%, 10% and 25% on devnet, and none of them reaches max_target. #96 then normalised the retarget against the window's AVERAGE target rather than its last one, which is what stabilises the controller against ordinary Poisson dispersion rather than against an attacker — before it, exponential arrivals with NO ATTACKER AT ALL reached max_target in a few hundred to a couple of thousand blocks. The pole arithmetic and the exactness argument for the mean live in the comment on pow.NextTarget, which is the one place they should be; the control is core/pow/honest_chain_poisson_test.go. WHAT THIS PARAMETER STILL DECIDES: lowering it bounds #70's push proportionally and tightens the honest-clock-skew tolerance by the same factor, and that trade is the whole choice it makes. A devnet was never a safety model for mainnet here and still is not — the exposure differs even where the rule does not. max_target (F-PARAM-1) remains the backstop of last resort in both directions, and a chain pinned at it is compromised rather than safe: BlockWork is 63 for every header there and fork choice degenerates toward a block count. Reproductions are in the header of sim/timestamp_test.go.
notes.min_base_fee: NOT the practical resting point. The base-fee decrease is a proportional step that integer division rounds to zero once the fee falls below base_fee_max_change_denominator, so a quiet chain settles at roughly that denominator rather than here. This matches EIP-1559 and is deterministic. min_base_fee is the hard floor, not the observed one (I1-L3).
notes.par_gas_ratio: The abundant resource: a fixed multiple of the sequential ceiling, so it grows only because that does. Priced cheap, so heavy cryptography does not compete with state mutation. CHEAP WAS INTENDED; INERT WAS NOT, and until #391 it was inert. At 10 the parallel break-even was par_gas_ratio*T0/block_byte_limit_genesis = 8.00 parallel gas per byte of block, against a densest legal Era-0 shape measuring 3.0352, so NextBaseFee only ever took its decrease branch: the parallel base fee walked to its resting point in four blocks and stayed there for the life of the chain, and B6 was dead code at every T. Both terms are linear in T, so no growth of the sequential target could ever have fixed it. At 3, on #392's 1,600,000 target base, the break-even is 1.92 and a byte-full block of ordinary payments applies 1.19x the parallel target, so the market has feedback from block 0. The owner's framing of the value is the accurate one: 3 is the same operating point already approved, re-denominated on the new target base. WHAT 3 DELIBERATELY DOES NOT BUY: B6 stays inert in Era 0. It requires 2*par_gas_ratio*T0/block_byte_limit_genesis = 3.84 parallel gas per byte of block, and Era-0 parallel density is bounded above by 3.0352 BY DERIVATION rather than by sample, AND THAT BOUND IS ATTAINED. The earlier 3.6242 treated the signature count s and the derive-unit count u as free of one another; they are not, because V4 refuses a signature that authorises nothing and requiredAddrs is the debited-or-burned addresses of the program plus the deposit cell, so s <= u + 1 at every Era-0 program kind. Put that coupling back and the densest shape is a RETIRE of max_sigs - 1 one-shot targets paying its deposit from a fresh persistent cell -- 3,804 bytes of body, 16 signatures, 11,558 parallel gas, 11558/3808 = 3.0352 in a block -- so the bound is derived and a witness meets it. RAISING max_sigs CANNOT REACH 3.84: under the coupled bound there is no crossing point, the ceiling only approaches gas_par_per_byte + (gas_par_per_sig + gas_par_per_derive_unit)/(32 + WriteSize + SigSize) = 3.1111 and never passes it at any setting of the list limits, so NO value of max_sigs makes B6 reachable at par_gas_ratio = 3 -- the earlier note solved its loose bound for a crossing at max_sigs = 35, which the coupled bound does not have. For the record, the loose form's own value was 3.6202, not 3.6242: 2 + (200s + 50u - 8)/(337 + 96s + 128u) at s = 16, u = 1 is 3.6202, and 3.6242 is that same expression with the -8 dropped. That B6 stays inert is accepted rather than overlooked: the intent is that B6 be alive for when the heavy cryptography of whitepaper 12 arrives, and a ceiling with headroom is what a ceiling should look like. Both figures are DERIVED and asserted against a witness in sim/block_ceiling_boundary_test.go -- era0ParDensityCeiling lands on 3.0352 with densestEra0Retire attaining it, and era0ParDensityLimit derives the 3.1111 limit that TestB6CannotFireOnAnyBlockTheByteCeilingAdmits pins at all three shipped sets -- so this note quotes a test rather than a measurement taken once.
notes.seq_gas_target_genesis: T₀: the initial value AND the permanent floor of the sequential target T (whitepaper §8.1). T is consensus state from block 0 (types.SeqGasTargetSlot), not a constant — the ceiling is 2T, the burst bound is 4T, and this number is only where T starts and how low it can ever fall. 1,600,000 rather than 2,000,000 since #392, and the reason is calibration and not capacity — block_byte_limit_genesis carries the break-even arithmetic. GENESIS THROUGHPUT DOES NOT MOVE, because it was never gas-bound: the byte ceiling still admits the same block and 8.1's ~90 applied certificates per second, and the elastic curve is unchanged. Three things downstream do move, each recorded where it is measured: B5 becomes reachable ON DENSITY, at 2.56 sequential gas per byte of block instead of 3.2 -- though since #586 the signature ceiling B18 binds first on every shape that supplies that density, so density is no longer sufficient (max_certs_per_block_genesis); the count ceiling and the 2T soft threshold coincide at the encoding floor (same note); and seq_gas_capacity follows at the pinned ratio to 5,120,000.
notes.max_certs_per_block_genesis: The certificate-count ceiling at genesis. MaxCertsPerBlock(T) scales it by T/seq_gas_target_genesis and clamps it to cert_list_capacity, so this number is where the ceiling starts and whitepaper §8.1's whole curve carries it upward with its ratio to block_byte_limit_genesis unchanged. IT IS NOT A CAPACITY POLICY AND IT IS NOT MEANT TO BIND FOR ORDINARY TRAFFIC. It bounds the certificate list's width -- checked before ComputeCertRoot, because ssz.Merkleize panics rather than errors on an oversized list -- and the one question it answers is how large a flood of the CHEAPEST certificates the Era-0 program set admits may be. That is the case bytes do not bound, because minimum-size certificates are exactly the ones bytes are cheap for. THE ENCODING FLOOR IS 558 BYTES AND TWO SHAPES REACH IT, not one: a RETIRE of a single one-shot address whose deposit cell is that same address (swept), and a RETIRE of a single one-shot address whose deposit cell is the PERSISTENT TWIN of the same key -- the twin is not one-shot so no second MARK_SPENT is derived, and V4 matches on the public key so one signature authorises both roles. Both are 558 encoded bytes, 562 in a block once the four offset bytes EncodeVariableList writes per element are counted, 800 sequential gas. Nothing smaller can be built: 328 bytes of fixed certificate fields, one 96-byte signature (V1 requires at least one), a 37-byte program header and address, and the single 97-byte MARK_SPENT every program derives are all unavoidable. THE CEILING AT THE OTHER END IS DERIVED FROM THE PARAMETERS RATHER THAN MEASURED FROM A SHAPE SEARCH, AND IT IS THE NUMBER A SECOND IMPLEMENTATION SHOULD SIZE AGAINST. The widest certificate a conforming decoder must accept follows from the decode limits and the encoding alone: 328 bytes of fixed certificate fields, plus the widest program body -- 5 bytes of program header plus max(128 x max_moves_per_transfer, 32 x max_retire_addrs) -- plus 97 x max_reads, plus 97 x max_writes, plus 96 x max_sigs. At the genesis values that is 328 + 4101 + 6208 + 6208 + 1536 = 18,381 bytes of certificate BODY and 18,385 in a block. UnmarshalCertificate enforces every one of those limits, so nothing above this decodes at all, and the figure MOVES WHEN THOSE LIMITS OR THE FIELD WIDTHS MOVE instead of going stale in silence. IT IS AN UPPER BOUND AND IT IS NOT CLAIMED TO BE ATTAINED: no single program saturates the read, write, signature and program limits at once. SIZE BUFFERS AND VALIDATION LIMITS AGAINST IT AND NOT AGAINST ANY MEASURED SHAPE. The reason is PROTOCOL.md rule 21, and this note is one of the places that got it wrong: the widest Era-0 certificate has been published three times and been wrong three times -- 7,823 bytes, then 10,125 (the widest member of the sweep described below, and the figure THIS NOTE ITSELF CARRIED), then 13,699 of body and 13,703 in a block -- each falsified by a corner the previous search could not see, because the binding constraint is max_writes = 64 rather than max_sigs or max_moves_per_transfer and the optimum is INTERIOR to a constrained region of several dimensions rather than on any one named axis. THE TRUE MAXIMUM CERTIFICATE WIDTH IS NARROWER THAN THAT SAFE BUFFER, AND SINCE #448/#472 IT IS A MAXIMUM BY DERIVATION RATHER THAN A LOWER BOUND BY SEARCH: 15,277 bytes of body and 15,281 in a block, DERIVED AND ATTAINED -- a TRANSFER of 32 moves drawn from 32 source cells (16 one-shot addresses and the 16 persistent twins of the same keys, one signature authorising both roles under V4) into only 16 DISTINCT destinations, so the 32 credits merge into 16 write slots and leave room for the 32 debits and 16 MARK_SPENTs that fill max_writes exactly, at 32 reads and 16 signatures. THE COUPLINGS THE 18,385 FORM OMITS ARE WHAT MAKE 15,281 ATTAINED RATHER THAN MERELY BOUNDED: V3 forces reads and writes to exactly what validity.Derive emits, so a TRANSFER's reads are one per DISTINCT debited slot with R <= min(m, max_reads) and m <= max_moves_per_transfer = 32; V4 forces the signature count to the distinct keys the body needs, S <= min(max_sigs, m+1); and RETIRE derives no reads while AddressFromPubKey is injective, so a retire's width is capped by max_sigs well before max_retire_addrs. era0CertByteCeiling puts those couplings back over the integers the V-rules admit and widestEra0Transfer builds a certificate of exactly 15,281 in a block; sim/block_ceiling_boundary_test.go's TestTheWidestEra0CertificateIsDerivedAndAttained asserts the two meet at all three shipped sets, and a later sweep of 794,341 admissible shapes -- including the DISTINCT DESTINATION COUNT, non-native-asset and alternative-deposit axes the earlier searches never varied -- found nothing above it. THE DIMENSION EVERY EARLIER SEARCH MISSED WAS DISTINCT DESTINATION COUNT: merging destinations buys back the write budget those searches spent, and it is the one none of the three superseded maxima varied. THERE IS NO FIFTH NUMBER -- the only remaining axis is a parameter, not a shape -- so 15,281 MOVES WHEN max_writes, max_sigs, max_moves_per_transfer or the field widths move instead of going stale, exactly as the 18,385 safe buffer does. THE PER-CERTIFICATE BUDGET IS NOT block_byte_limit_genesis DIVIDED BY THIS VALUE: a block spends 236 bytes on itself and four more per certificate out of the same ceiling, so at genesis the budget is (2500000-236)/4000 - 4 = 620.9 bytes of certificate BODY, not 625. THE COUNT CEILING AND THE 2T SOFT THRESHOLD NOW COINCIDE AT THE ENCODING FLOOR, exactly: the count rule admits 4000 certificates and 2T admits 2*1,600,000/800 = 4000 of the 800-gas floor certificate, so a block filled to the count ceiling with floor certificates declares precisely 2T of sequential gas -- at F11's forfeiture threshold, where the quadratic is zero, and never above it. Under the superseded T0 of 2,000,000 the same block declared 1.6T and the two bounds had a fifth of margin between them. NOTHING IS REJECTED THAT WAS NOT REJECTED BEFORE; what is gone is the margin, and the visible consequence is in spec/gen, where the mainnet count-ceiling vector's ceiling+1 block is now above 2T at every T and its guard is stated against 4T instead. TWO SEQUENTIAL-GAS BOUNDS EXIST AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME BOUND. core/fold/blockrules.go rejects a block only above SeqGasBurst(T) = 4T; a block between 2T and 4T is valid and F11 forfeits producer subsidy against it quadratically. So 4T is the block-validity ceiling and 2T is a SOFT threshold -- the fee market's target ceiling, priced rather than enforced. Measured over 98 distinct shapes swept along the NAMED AXES of the Era-0 shape space (retire width x deposit arrangement, transfer move count x source address version, issue and mint x deposit cell), all built through wallet.Builder and validity-clean -- A SAMPLE AND NOT A CENSUS, which is why the ceiling above is stated in derived form and the maximum width as a derived bound a witness attains rather than as a swept figure: under the 4T bound that actually rejects, the ceilings split the space into exactly THREE classes with no ties -- COUNT binds for the two 558 B floor shapes, GAS binds for 38, and BYTES binds for the other 58; NO shape is parallel-bound. THE GAS CLASS IS NEW AT THESE PARAMETERS AND IT IS WHAT MADE B5 REACHABLE: under the superseded T0 = 2,000,000 the 4T bound demanded 3.2 sequential gas per byte of block against a densest achievable 2.8937, so the class was empty and no block could be refused by B5 at all (#395); at T0 = 1,600,000 it demands 2.56 and 38 already-built shapes clear it. B5 IS NO LONGER REACHABLE ON THAT CLASS, AND THE REASON IS max_sigs_per_block_genesis (#586): the gas class is made of RETIRE-family shapes that spend ONE SIGNATURE PER 706 SEQUENTIAL GAS, so a block dense enough to reach 4T declares more signatures than B18 admits and B18 -- checked before the loop that verifies a signature, and therefore before B5 -- answers first. The largest block of the gas-densest family B18 admits reaches 66% of 4T. THAT IS NOT A CLAIM THAT B5 IS UNREACHABLE: it is measured on the family that used to witness it, no census of the shape space exists, and this note's own history is four published shape maxima and four falsifications. B5 remains a rule an implementation must enforce, with no golden vector to catch it, like B11 and B16; core/fold's TestB18BindsBeforeB5OnTheGasDensestFamily is where the measurement lives. That is an existential over shapes that exist rather than a claim about shapes nobody has built. The count rule is still the only rejecting ceiling that binds the floor: without it the minimum-size flood would be bounded at 4447 by bytes and 8000 by 4T gas instead of 4000. Under the 2T soft threshold the gas class widens to 76 of the 98 shapes, the gas-densest being a RETIRE of 15 addresses paying its deposit from a fresh one-shot cell at 2.897 sequential gas per byte -- but that is F11's price on a revenue-maximising producer, not a rule any block is rejected for, and an earlier revision of this note wrongly called it a third block ceiling. 4000 IS REACHABLE AND IT IS NOT AN ALL-RETIRE CURIOSITY (#145): a block of 4000 floor certificates is 2,248,236 bytes, 89.93% of the byte ceiling, and the slack pays for up to 868 ordinary one-move transfers beside 3,132 retires (2,499,956 bytes; 869 is 2,500,246 and does not fit) -- 21.7% of the block by certificate count and 29.6% by bytes. The rule also FIRES rather than merely being reachable: a ceiling+1 block of floor certificates fits under the byte ceiling at every T, with 251,202 bytes of slack at the tightest (T0 itself). THE BYTE UTILISATION IS NOT CONSTANT IN T. Both ceilings floor independently -- the count steps once per 500 units of T while bytes step 1.25 per unit -- so utilisation dips just before each count step. Measured at EVERY integer T in [T0, seq_gas_capacity]: 89.9070% at the worst (T=1,600,399) and 89.9294% at the best (T=T0); on the maximal growth ladder T <- T + T/512 the first rung after genesis is already 89.9112%. A sweep that steps by 1000 from the superseded T0 of 2,000,000 sampled only exact divisions and reported [89.92%, 89.93%], which is how an earlier revision of this note got the interval wrong; the interval above is swept one unit at a time and does not rest on that. THE VALUE'S BAND HAS TWO DIFFERENT UPPER EDGES AND CONFLATING THEM IS AN ERROR THIS NOTE MADE ONCE. At T0 the band is [2933, 4447]: at 4448 no block at T0 reaches the ceiling, and below 2933 the count ceiling starts cutting the byte-bound capacity of ordinary payments (whitepaper §15's 2,900-certificate block, 2,471,036 bytes here, survives down to 2900 and is cut only below that). But a genesis value unreachable at T0 can become reachable further up the curve, because both ceilings floor independently: 4448 first becomes violable at T=1,687,410, where MaxCertsPerBlock is 4690 and a 4691-certificate block is exactly the 2,636,578-byte ceiling. It is not a lone T either -- 1,469,202 of the 3,520,001 reachable values (41.74%) are violable at that genesis value, including 7,316 of the 17,601 multiples of 200, the first at T=1,744,600. Multiples of 200 are the ones that matter: every Era-0 gas constant is a multiple of 100, so a median applied figure is too, and NextSeqGasTarget's 2*median input is therefore a multiple of 200. DO NOT ARGUE THIS FROM THE MAXIMAL GROWTH LADDER, which an earlier revision did and got wrong in both directions: T <- T + T/512 PASSES 1,687,410 at rung 28, but jumps straight over the violable band there -- rung 28 is T=1,689,835, whose ceiling+1 block is 145 bytes over its ceiling -- and the first ladder rung that is actually violable is 77, at T=1,859,350. Rung 28 answers when T passes the threshold; rung 77 answers when the rule could first fire on that one path; the 41.74% answers the question the parameter choice turns on. 4449 IS THE FIRST VALUE INERT AT EVERY REACHABLE T. Both bands and both edges are armed in core/fold/cert_budget_test.go, so a change to this value, to the byte ceiling, to the gas schedule or to the certificate encoding fails the build with the recomputed figures instead of converting this rule into something else quietly. Devnet is deliberately not calibrated this way: 256 against the same byte ceiling makes the count rule the operative bound for 97 of the same 98 shapes -- all but the widest one-shot-source TRANSFER IN THAT SWEEP, which is byte-bound because its 10,129 bytes IN A BLOCK (10,125 of body plus its offset) exceed devnet's 9,764.70-byte in-block budget, or equivalently its 10,125-byte body exceeds the 9,760.70-byte body budget. THAT SHAPE IS THE SWEEP'S WIDEST AND NOT THE WIDEST; the split survives the difference, because a certificate wider than it is more byte-bound rather than less and so joins the same class instead of moving between them. Both units appear in this file and they differ by the four offset bytes; the mainnet 620.9 figure above is a BODY budget. Count-bound almost everywhere is what a development network wants.
notes.max_sigs_per_block_genesis: The per-block SIGNATURE ceiling at genesis, and the operative bound on receiver-side verification cost (#586). MaxSigsPerBlock(T) scales it by T/seq_gas_target_genesis exactly as MaxCertsPerBlock does, and core/fold checks the sum of the block's certificate signature counts against it (B18) BEFORE any signature is verified -- a ceiling consulted after the work it bounds bounds nothing. IT EXISTS BECAUSE gas_par_per_sig CANNOT BOUND AND PRICE AT THE SAME TIME. That parameter has two consumers: it bounds verification per block through ParGasLimit, and it prices the parallel fee market as parallel-gas density per byte, which is what NextBaseFee compares against the target. The pre-launch audit measured one strict Ed25519 verification at ~734 microseconds against a schedule calibrated as if it were ~15x cheaper, and recommended recalibrating gas_par_per_sig to ~3000. THAT RECALIBRATION WAS TESTED AND REJECTED. At ~3000 the derived Era-0 parallel density limit 2 + (gas_par_per_sig + gas_par_per_derive_unit)/225 moves from 3.1111 to 15.56, crossing B6's 3.84 inertness threshold, so assertB6IsInertByDerivation fails -- and fails CORRECTLY, because the deliberate inertness the par_gas_ratio note documents stops holding. An ordinary transfer's parallel density moves 2.23 -> 5.52 gas per byte, so a byte-full block of ordinary payments applies ~2.9x the parallel target instead of the 1.19x #391/#392 calibrated, and at base_fee_max_change_denominator = 8 the parallel base fee climbs 12.5% per block under the network's own design load -- the market #392 fixed responding backwards again, from the other side. Compensating with par_gas_ratio ~= 7 restores 1.19x and re-opens the ceiling to ~7,500 signatures. The two requirements pull one parameter in opposite directions: A MODELING ERROR, NOT A VALUE ERROR, and no number resolves it. So gas_par_per_sig STAYS AT 200 and the bound gets a parameter of its own. THE AUDIT'S 48,000 SIGNATURES / ~86 CORE-SECONDS IS NOT REACHABLE, and the correction matters because it is the number that would have justified the recalibration. 48,000 divides ParGasLimit alone; a signature is 96 encoded bytes, so 48,000 of them need >= 4.6 MB of signature bytes against a 2.5 MB byte ceiling -- THE BYTE CEILING BINDS LONG BEFORE THE PARALLEL ONE. The densest legal shape (16 signatures in 3,808 in-block bytes, the same witness the par_gas_ratio note derives) admits ~656 certificates ~= ~10,500 signatures per block before the 4T sequential bound trims it further, so the worst case without this ceiling is ~7.7 core-seconds per 30-second block -- ~26% of the interval on one core, 2.6x the honest maximum, an order of magnitude short of ~86. WHY 6000. The HONEST maximum is 4,000 signatures: a count-bound block of single-signature floor certificates, max_certs_per_block_genesis of them. A byte-bound block of ordinary transfers carries 2,933. 6000 is 1.5x honest, so no honest traffic mix is refused -- a multi-signature RETIRE burst just packs across more blocks, as it would under any ceiling -- while the adversarial worst case falls ~10,500 -> 6,000 signatures, ~4.4 core-seconds, ~15% of the interval. THE PRECEDENT IS BITCOIN'S MAX_BLOCK_SIGOPS: a per-block signature-operation ceiling distinct from the byte limit, in production since July 2010 and carried through segwit as MAX_BLOCK_SIGOPS_COST = 80,000. Price and ceiling are different questions and get different numbers. SIZED AS IF VerifyStrict IS NEVER OPTIMIZED. In-tree ZIP-215-style verification over a dedicated Edwards field implementation is endorsed as post-launch work under its own audit, with bit-identical accept/reject decisions as the acceptance bar; if it lands, 6000 becomes merely conservative, which is the safe side of wrong. NOTHING ELSE MOVED FOR IT: the derived density constants, the witness tests in sim/block_ceiling_boundary_test.go, B6's inertness and the #391/#392 market operating point are all untouched. THIS IS ALSO THE BOUND ON #585's DROP-STUFFING: a block filled to every ceiling with certificates that deterministically DROP costs receivers at most 6,000 strict verifications regardless of what V5 declares, which is the sig-count x strict-verify product the audit asked for, capped by construction and no longer growing when the byte ceilings grow.
notes.block_byte_limit_genesis: The block-size ceiling at genesis; BlockByteLimit(T) scales it by T/seq_gas_target_genesis and clamps it to block_byte_capacity. This is the ceiling that binds for the traffic the network actually carries: measured over the same 98-shape sweep along named axes that max_certs_per_block_genesis describes -- a sample and not a census -- under the 4T bound block validity rejects on, it is the first ceiling to bind for 96 of those 98 shapes, everything except the two 558-byte floor shapes, which are count-bound. A block of ordinary payments is byte-bound at 2933 one-move transfers long before it is count-bound at 4000. It is therefore this parameter, and not the count ceiling, that carries whitepaper §8.1's genesis throughput claim of '~90 applied certificates per second (a §15 block per 30-second interval)' -- §15's block of 2,900 certificates at the payment shape is 2,471,036 bytes here, 98.8% of the ceiling. Whether the pair (this, seq_gas_target_genesis) is well calibrated against real traffic was open until #392 and is now DECIDED, by lowering the target rather than by raising this ceiling: the break-even is seq_gas_target_genesis/block_byte_limit_genesis = 0.64 sequential gas per byte OF BLOCK, and the density it is compared against has to be measured in the same units -- a plain transfer is 600 gas in 852 bytes of block (848 of body plus its 4 offset bytes) = 0.704, not the 0.708 that body-only accounting gives. 0.704 sits ABOVE 0.64 with 9.1% of margin, so a physically full block of simple payments -- 2933 certificates applying 1,759,800 gas -- applies 1.0999 of the target and pushes the sequential base fee UP, which is whitepaper 8.1's own calibration rule. Until #392 the target was 2,000,000, the break-even was 0.8, the same block applied 0.880, and the market responded BACKWARDS to the load the paper says the network is built for. THE MARGIN IS WHY 1,600,000 AND NOT 1,700,000: these densities have already moved about 1% twice under re-derivation, and this number has no repair path after block 0. It was not left to the testnet because it cannot be: it is in the ConsensusRoot, so a testnet carrying a different value measures a different chain. See max_certs_per_block_genesis for the count ceiling, the 2T-versus-4T distinction, and how the ceilings split the shape space.
notes.cert_list_capacity: A structural bound, not a policy one: fixes the SSZ decode limit and CertRoot's merkle padding width. Cannot move with T — a capacity that changed with height would make one certificate list hash to different roots at different heights — and unlike the byte and gas capacities it cannot be re-pinned cleanly at an era boundary either, because a re-pin changes what a certificate list hashes to and so puts two merkle widths in one chain. It is therefore the one capacity sized at genesis for the whole curve of whitepaper 8.1 rather than for the launch network, and it is where the ladder ends: 2^25 = 33,554,432 certificates is 1,118,481 per second at 30-second blocks, which maximal ceiling growth from the genesis rate of ~88 reaches in 13.6 years only across era re-pins of seq_gas_capacity (whitepaper 8.1's third condition): within any one era T is clamped at seq_gas_capacity, so the count ceiling is bounded by max_certs_per_block_genesis × seq_gas_capacity / seq_gas_target_genesis — 12,800 at this file's values, 2,621x below this capacity — and only an era boundary moves that wall. Size it against the curve's end and not its ten-year mark — an earlier revision used 2^22, whose 139,810 per second the same growth reaches in 10.6 years under the same cross-era ladder, putting a wall no era can move just past the horizon the paper claims. The padding is virtual (zero-subtree hashing), so the cost of the headroom is the tree's depth — 25 levels against the 16 a 2^16 capacity needed — and nothing else, and the decode limit it also fixes is dominated by block_byte_capacity, since a claimed list needs four offset bytes per element present in the payload. max_certs_per_block_genesis must not exceed it.
notes.block_byte_capacity: The hard ceiling block_byte_limit_genesis scales toward, and the reason it exists is transport, not policy: a block consensus calls valid must still be one every node can move within a block interval. Unclamped, the byte ceiling follows T forever, and T rises at its maximum rate whenever demand fills the target — which under a working fee market is continuously, not only under attack — so from the genesis values it would outrun what the transport carries in roughly 620 epochs. The failure mode is the bad one: not a rejected block but a block every node agrees is valid and no node can transmit. Blocks travel as chunks (node/p2p wire.go), so no single frame bounds this value; what bounds it is the chunked-transfer ceiling MaxBlockChunks x BlockChunkBytes, and TestBlockByteCapacityFitsChunkedTransfer pins that pair together. This is the capacity an era boundary re-pins (whitepaper 8.1) against measured propagation, together with seq_gas_capacity at the fixed genesis ratio; the accompanying node release raises the transport constants through the same test.
notes.max_cites_per_block: Bounds the competing-header citations a block may carry for §8.1's health signal. Static for the same structural reason as cert_list_capacity: a merkle/decode capacity, not a demand-scaled ceiling.
notes.ceiling_growth_divisor: Γ. T grows by at most T/Γ per epoch when demand and the health gate both allow it — 512 compounds to at most a doubling per year of full blocks (whitepaper §8.1).
notes.ceiling_decay_divisor: Δ. T shrinks by at most T/Δ per epoch of low demand, and never below seq_gas_target_genesis — 1024 halves idle capacity in about two years.
notes.health_gate_bps: The epoch's cited-competing-header rate, in basis points of epoch_length, above which growth (never decay, never the floor) is withheld for the epoch. 200 = 2%, and the gate leans toward caution on purpose.
notes.skip_fee: A protocol constant, never a market price (R1-H1). Constancy is what makes the deposit ceiling statelessly checkable — and it is also why applied gas, not included gas, drives the base fees (R2-H2).
notes.ttl_max: Bounds seen-set lifetime (R1-H4) AND the fee-drift window a signer must buffer against (R2-H1). Raising it makes both worse; it is not a free latency knob.
notes.seq_gas_capacity: The ceiling T itself may never pass, and the third structural bound after cert_list_capacity and block_byte_capacity. It exists because clamping only the DERIVED ceilings leaves T free to climb to twice what a full block can hold, where the base-fee target sits above anything a block can deliver and the sequential market stops pricing entirely. Its value is not a free choice: it must preserve the genesis ratio, seq_gas_capacity/seq_gas_target_genesis == block_byte_capacity/block_byte_limit_genesis, so gas and bytes reach their walls together and the terminal state prices exactly like block 0. Validate enforces that as a cross-multiplication.
